inline.s: Fragrant trees, early summer's growth; / a light boat on jade-green lake water. / I carry my lute to seek an old friend — / where, in clouds so deep, to find him?
Across the broken bridge a figure goes; / a little boat beneath the frosty moon. / I turn my head to the cloud-wrapped hills: / all the world of dust is shut away.
Misty trees and spring clouds, green; / river and sky, a red setting sun. / Who knows where he has gone to drink? / He will come home in the bright moonlight.
A lone boat in a night of wind and rain; / the faint, dim blur of grass and trees in spring. / A dog barks, startled, under the thatch eaves — / it must be someone crossing the river.
Fine clouds drift past the river pavilion; / a lonely village lies idle in the daylight. / A small bridge spans the wild water, / cutting off ten thousand ranges of hills.
I sit at peace in the peach-blossom hollow; / my quiet dwelling is far from the market's dust. / Only because spring's colors are fair — / not to flee the Qin.
In the tall trees the new cicadas shrill; / deep woods hide a thatched hut. / Across the broken bridge a figure goes; / white clouds fill the whole valley.
A waterfall falls beyond the cold sky; / a lone pavilion among water and stone. / The days are long, with not a thing to do — / I take a companion to look at spring hills.
Autumn water, green as jade; / far mountains congealed like cream. / Deep in the night the fish do not bite — / for whom is the bait cast?

With a patter and sigh the cold woods grow lean; / with a purl and murmur the water and stones run clear. / White clouds for a thousand, ten thousand miles — / gazing at each other, we simply forget all feeling.
Over ten thousand trees the clouds stream thick; / on a thousand peaks the setting light grows cold. / My rustic gate stays shut the livelong day; / at dusk I look to the one who shares my wine.
Far trees merge into the clear-day mist; / the river opens out, the grass pavilion cold. / I chant as I walk, one with the riverside — / only now I believe how hard it is to stay sober alone.
Old trees, grey pines grown ancient; / clear springs and white stones, rare and strange. / I carry my lute to seek a kindred soul — / far off I see a tavern's banner.
Seated in the river pavilion, I forget all contrivance; / leaning on the rail, I watch the evening light. / Someone stands waiting on the sandbar, / meaning to go home when the moon comes up.
White clouds; the sky trails silk. / The river clears, its water one with space. / Hand in hand we seek a drinking friend / and cross together east of the stone bridge.
On autumn hills the cloud-breath thins; / against red trees the dawn frost lies clear. / A single stretch of lake and sky, wide open — / left empty, waiting for the moon.
The hills are like the road to Mount Tiantai; / the blossoms hold no spring of Qin. / A fisherman sits at the mouth of the creek — / no one comes to ask the way.
Red clouds, and all four fields blotted out; / layer on layer of ice, ten thousand trees snapped. / Braving the cold, I go to visit an old friend, / trampling through the linked snow of the hills.
Ten thousand hills congealed in piled snow; / on the tall trees the light ice breaks. / Where does the cold-season plum come into bloom? / Its fragrance draws one monk after it.
Autumn hills, the new rain clearing; / far waters calm and boundless. / On the lake a recluse has his dwelling, / as high and far as the world's dust.
The Dream Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Forty-Nine
Meeting He Xuanpu at Nanyue
We meet before the Southern Peak; / we sit facing the mid-autumn moon. / Its clear light we watch the whole night through, / wondering if it is the snow on Yan Mountain.
Yushan
At leisure I climb to the top of Yushan; / in the city I see smoke and fire. / Ten thousand rooftops crowd like clouds — / each a blue lotus blossom.
The River-Viewing Tower
Alone I climb the River-Viewing Tower; / on every side the hills are woven like cloth. / Among them lives one who feeds on cloud-haze — / we face each other, and do not know each other.
High Mountain Temple
The mountain town pillows the flowing river; / the temple rises up out of the clouds. / A bell sounds, and ten thousand doors open; / people are walking inside the lotus.
Fool's Creek
How is Fool's Creek like me? / I am the fool; the creek is not. / Its spring waters sound by day and night — / the sound of Dharma, murmuring low.
Huayan Hermitage
The hermitage stands near the Ganges' water; / a monk's robe, and the city of Sravasti. / The sound of sutras mingles with human speech: / they are always preaching the unborn.
Miscellaneous Verses, Two Poems
The white crane flies, soaring to the sky, / free and untrammelled, going or staying as it will. / Pity this unimpeded body — / it does not know the road of birth and death.
Ants crave what is rank and raw; / chasing an odor, they call to their fellows. / Hurrying, hurrying, never pausing — / and what do they gain in the end?
Impromptu, Two Poems
My Dharma companions, a thousand peak-shadows; / my livelihood, a few acres of field. / Truly I know: within this human world / such a bond is hard to make.
Green hills wait for a man's return. / I meant to seek a deep accord; / who would have thought the newcomer's heart / would clash with me in every move and stillness?
Mountain Dwelling, Thirteen Poems
A single cloud floats in the vast void; / in a moment it spreads over the whole earth. / Try to look at the state before you were born — / pure and still, without a speck of dust.
All ten thousand scenes are still by nature; / it is the mind that makes them rise and cease. / If a single thought does not arise, / where can you go to find stillness or motion?
Through the long night there is no lamp or candle; / the road ahead lies altogether dark. / Pitiful are those who sleep so soundly — / when will they wake from the great dream?
Into green mountains it is easy to enter; / pure karma is not hard to cultivate. / Only the art of stilling the mind — / there even heroes yield a step.
One pillow, the dream of yellow millet; / a thousand years of bloody merit. / Men only know such glory should endure for ever — / who believes it all turns empty in a moment?
Old snow, and grey pines grown ancient; / a monk at leisure, water and stones clear. / Sitting here, a hundred cares are forgotten; / I see this body suddenly grow light.
The fierce heat is past bearing; / a pure breeze comes down through the bamboo. / With a rustle and a sigh cool air rises — / marrow and bone are suddenly refreshed.
The wind falls still; the cicadas cry the faster. / The dragon returns, and the rain-smell is rank. / I take the cool beneath the tall trees / and idly copy the Goose-Swapping Sutra.
Where the clouds are deep there is a wild temple; / the old monk loves to lean upon his staff. / He comes back late from begging his food, / dreading to thread ten miles of pine.
Crisp air enters the sparse woods; / on ten thousand hills the autumn colors are fair. / Greedy to watch the clouds at the creek's head, / I forget the road by which I came.
I sit alone beneath the tall pine, / calm with the heart of highest antiquity. / High hills and flowing streams, such is my thought — / who is there left to understand the note?
Sun and moon, like flying birds; / heaven and earth, like a rolling ball. / This floating life is spent in busy haste — / who will look at it from within stillness?
One bowl of ever-burning lamp; / facing it at night, the heart grows stiller. / How many are the wine-sodden sleepers / whose mad dreams in sleep have never ceased?
Mountain Dwelling, Twenty Poems (Six-Character Lines)
Under the pines, a few rafters of thatch; / before my eyes, green hills on every side. / Sun and moon rise and sink without resting; / white clouds come and go, always at ease.
In the snow the plum blossom first opens; / a hidden fragrance drifts in late at night. / Just as I sit alone facing the cold lamp, / it suddenly blasts my nostrils open.
A few flakes of white cloud that will not leave; / a single round of bright moon that comes flying in. / They keep me company in the mountains' loneliness; / I laugh at the dust of the world below.

A single stretch of cold heart on a snowy night; / a few strokes of the frost bell that shatter dreams. / In the stove the incense dies to lingering embers; / beyond the window the moon climbs a lonely peak.

My whole face is covered in biting clear frost; / my whole head is white hair, sighing and thin. / In the world, empty flowers drop their shadows; / in my eyes the cataracts of illusion are wholly gone.
With a patter the spring's voice enters my ears; / bright and plain, the Ancestor's meaning comes from the West. / Unmoving, the tongue's root speaks always — / what need to sigh again, How wondrous!
In the hidden valley the orchid's fragrance is rich; / at midnight the moonlight is fair and fine. / A single stretch of clear dust stirs and swells — / and for no reason dry meditation is broken.
One thought forgets its conditions, utterly still; / a solitary brightness shines alone, wide awake. / See through it: lightning in the empty sky — / not at all the firefly before your eyes.

The clouds scatter in the vast sky, the rain has passed; / the snow melts in the cold valley, and spring is born. / I only feel this body washed as if in water; / I do not know the mind is clear as ice.
Decayed and old, one pities these weak bones; / yet looking on, I find the mind grown strong. / At midnight the backbone is like iron; / at all other hours one thought is like frost.
In the empty valley all dust is wholly dismissed; / only a single scrap of idle cloud remains. / It keeps me company as I wield my whisk by the pine roots — / how good that the deer gather in herds.
Letters are a cataract in the eye; / dhyana is a floating mote upon the mind. / Take up both, inside and out, and cast them off — / the whole body is the great chiliocosm.
In the still night the bell does not stop sounding; / on the stone bed, dreams and imaginings are all empty. / I open my eyes and do not know where I am — / I only hear my ears full of pine wind.
Pure and clear, a precious mirror holding the void; / when spring comes, the water fills Peng Lake. / It shines through to the true face of Mount Lu — / the moon is a bright pearl on the brow.

The lotus water-clock's six hours still seem short; / long incense is set to burn a hundred marks. / Day and night the true and constant flows and pours — / the conscious spirit has long been lodged in the lotus womb.
A single cloud seals the valley's mouth; / a thousand peaks split the empty sky. / Among them are a few rafters of thatch, / hiding deep a white-haired mountain elder.
How sad that green hills always remain; / how I sigh that white hair comes ever new. / We are all wayfarers within the dust — / who is the idler beyond all things?
The mountain's look is sad with last night's rain; / the pine's voice chokes cold in the clear frost. / A begging monk, like a weary bird; / the crescent moon puts on new makeup.
The world's light is like water and moon; / body and mind are bright as lapis lazuli. / I only see the ice melt at the ravine's bottom — / I do not know spring has come to the flowering branch.
Outside the gate, green hills bloom one by one; / before the window, yellow leaves rustle and sigh. / I sit alone, with nothing to say — / turning back, I see deluded thoughts wholly gone.
Immediate Matters Aboard the Boat

Empty water joins the sky, and one leaf of a boat; / I look at once on this life as a floating bubble. / A wild goose's cry shatters the dream of dependent birth; / bright moon on the reeds at the old ferry crossing.
Mount Dagu

Cloud haze her skirt, cloud her robe, the moon her arched brow; / river and lake fill my eyes, and few are the friends I know. / The cold current runs to the bottom, the heart washed clean — / ask nothing of what husband she may be.
The Pagoda on Mount Gu
A pagoda in the void, a body of water and moon; / a single mote of dust set in the vast emptiness. / The traveler's two eyes are given another speck of chaff — / how many men can recognize the real?
Baotuo Temple on Lake Poyang
A palace of glass, a platter of crystal; / on every side green hills and jade-green rails. / Within it there is one who is always preaching: / he drains the Western River, the cold night tide.
Crossing the Tong River, Mourning Zeng Jianzhai, Chief of the Imperial Table

Beneath the Dragon Flower Tree we met of old; / every night we talked until we heard the dawn bell. / Today I look for you on the Tong River's waters — / in vain I hold back tears of blood in the spring wind.
Fisherman's Songs of the Clear River, Two Poems

The water clear, the sand white, the moon a hook; / its shadow falls on the wave's heart, the line not yet drawn in. / There are endless fish that cannot swallow the bait — / in vain the fisherman hugs his deep sorrow.

A single leaf of a boat tosses after the waves; / on the Five Lakes, wind and moon are free for the feasting. / Dream and soul are always in the deepest place; / the bitterest is leaving the hook, with the water colder still.
Mooring at Hengpu

Five clouds and a single river lead into Nan'an; / a thousand folded ranges turn back through the six-and-sixty rapids. / I walk on to where the water fails and the hills run out — / countless plum blossoms to be seen from the ridge.
Climbing the Wall of Nan'an

On the city wall, petal by petal, blue lotuses spring up; / in the flower's heart fragrance holds the smoke of ten thousand homes. / My body is inside a mirror, and no one knows me — / should I seek the heavens anywhere beyond this?
Crossing the Dayu Ridge, Two Poems

A single path through cloud and haze, the plank road deep; / plum blossoms and pine rain, the air dark and heavy. / I turn it over: those who traveled this way by night of old — / how do they compare with my heart crossing the ridge today?

On the ridge the cold plum is just coming into bloom; / the branches are wrapped in clouds like an old monk's robe. / Let me try lifting my staff and holding it out again — / its fragrance follows the heaven's wind to the world's edge.
Paying Respects to the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi, Two Poems

A drop of Caoxi's water comes from a wondrous source; / it flows into the blue sea, and the waves beat the sky. / How many fish and dragons are transformed along the way — / yet the single pulse at the source is still clear and cold.

No sooner had he cast down the woodcutter's axe than a stone fell on his waist; / at Huangmei, in the dead of night, he sat in silent emptiness. / Shouldering the Dharma, he went back south with a single bowl — / and from that time on his sons and grandsons grew prouder by the day.
On the Road to Guangzhou, Two Poems

Through misty waters I journeyed south through a hundred cities; / the good teachers I met were all without feeling. / No sooner had I drawn near, meaning to stay a moment, / than they pointed to the road ahead and took their leave.

The two banks and the midstream will not suffer me to stay; / my little boat follows the waves, at the mercy of the sky's wind. / I must simply hoist the lone sail high and go — / trusting that the wave of grace is the same everywhere.
Reaching the Garrison at Leiyang

Over the miasmal sea the mist floats day and night; / dragons and serpents breathe out vapor, muddying the clear stream. / When I arrive, the whole place is the land of the unborn — / all the more I see the ruler's grace is not easily repaid.
Sent to Reverend Wuyan of Shaolin, Two Poems

On the crest of Five Teats Peak the grass and trees grow deep; / when spring comes, blossoms open all through the empty woods. / On the summit the piled snow is still a thousand feet — / who now has a heart like the one who cut off his arm?

After the Qingliang assembly, back again to Chang'an; / each time we met, each time was joy. / Since we parted I gaze from the sky's south to the sky's north; / scorching wind and northern snow look on at one another.
Setting the Boat Loose on the Boluo River

A single sail goes east, the sea's waves calm; / flutes and drums sound as if from the heavens. / Far off I see the three mountains sink beyond the sky — / and do not know I am walking inside a mirror.
Sent to Master Zhen of Little Jinshan

The heaven's wind blows me up to the Wondrous High Terrace; / at midnight I ride the tide home, carrying the moon. / Sweep clean the stones on Mount Lanka — / wait for me to come again and copy out the sutra.
Little Jinshan, Three Poems

Ten thousand miles of long waves, flowing ten thousand miles; / who set a fistful of stone to stand against the midstream isle? / Had Yu not hewn the channel open in three tiers, / the fish and dragons would surely nod their heads in assent.

A crystal palace, cut off from every trace of dust; / fragrant mist and vapor, the dew-laden air thick. / In the empty sky the bright moon floats my guest-boat; / deep in the night fish and dragons lie at the steps.

The mountain floats on the water's face, the temple rests on emptiness; / its towers and halls are void, lost in the distant haze. / This is no conjured human world — / it must rather be a Brahma-king's palace risen from the sky.
Sent to Master Miaofeng of Hedong, Three Poems

The colors of Shouyang Mountain pillow the river's flow; / you, Master, dwell at the very summit of Zhongtiao. / Hemp fields before your bed, Zhang Jing's staff in hand — / to this day its grace makes ghosts and spirits grieve.

The Yellow River, a single thread, comes down from heaven; / it flows into the Central Plain and washes the ashes of the kalpa. / Grasp the crucial pass and watch the pillar in midstream — / the ship of compassion does not count mere river-crossing talent.

I have walked to the world's end, and the road is hard; / poisonous mists and scorching winds I have taken as my full meal. / Then suddenly I remember Longmen's thousand-fathom snow — / sharply it rises, and chills me to the heart.
Answering Grand Equerry Gao, Who Sent Incense

A single petal of famous incense from the high temple; / a sealed letter sent far to the scorched wilderness. / In dreams I hear the watch-gong and take it for a chime-stone; / rising at night, I burn it myself and bow to the Dharma King.
Longing for My Old Dwelling at Longmen on Mount Wutai
